Chapter Three: Crafting a Message That Resonates.
Now that you’ve got a clear idea of who your ideal customer is, let’s talk about building a message that really lands with them. It’s tempting for businesses to focus on themselves—their features, their backstory, maybe even a few shiny awards. But here’s the thing: most customers are tuned in to what matters to them, not to you.
So, effective marketing? It’s all about flipping the script. Instead of saying, “Look how great we are,” you want to speak directly to what your customers need, what they want, and especially what’s keeping them up at night.
Let me give you an example. Picture a bakery advertising “freshly baked bread daily.” Sure, that sounds nice, but it’s kind of generic, right? It could be any bakery anywhere. Now imagine if they said, “Warm, crusty loaves that make family dinners unforgettable.” Suddenly, you can see it—and probably even feel it. That message connects to an experience, not just a product.
Here’s the secret: you want to join the conversation that’s already happening in your customer’s mind. What are they worrying about? What are they hoping for? When you tap into these questions, your message becomes both relevant and hard to ignore.
There’s a simple approach to help you shape this kind of message:
First, identify the main problem your customer faces. What’s keeping them up at night?
Next, describe the outcome they really want. What’s their version of success?
Finally, bridge the gap. Show them how your product or service takes them from problem to solution.
For instance, a financial advisor could stick with, “We offer retirement planning services.” But that’s just information. It doesn’t connect. Instead, how about, “Helping busy professionals retire with confidence and peace of mind”? Now you’re speaking to their uncertainty—and the feeling of relief they’re looking for.
Storytelling is another powerful way to make your message stick. Share a quick, relatable story about how someone else benefited. Say you’re a landscaping company—you could talk about a family who turned their backyard into the go-to spot for summer gatherings. That paints a real picture and helps your listener imagine themselves enjoying the same thing.
To make sure your message really resonates, keep these three things in mind:
Make it clear—ditch the jargon.
Be specific—talk about a real problem or desire.
And go for emotion—reach for the heart, not just the head.
Don’t be afraid to test different messages and see what gets the best response. Listen to feedback and adjust. Over time, the best messages become the backbone for everything—from your website to social media to ads.
When you truly focus on what matters to your customer, you cut through the noise and make a real connection. Your message becomes a bridge, inviting the right people to take the next step with you.
